quiz.question: A pod is serving traffic correctly, but you wire the liveness probe to the same database health check as readiness. The database blips for 10 seconds. What happens?

options.A: kubelet kills the process and restarts the container, dropping in-flight work
options.B: Endpoints stay populated; only new connections are paused
options.C: The Deployment freezes rolling updates until the database recovers
options.D: kube-proxy retries the probe against a different replica

quiz.explanation: Liveness failure means 'this process is dead, restart it.' Tying liveness to a dependency turns a blip into a self-inflicted crash loop. Readiness should drop the pod from Endpoints; liveness should only catch a wedged process.

quiz.question: What is the correct split of responsibility between liveness and readiness?

options.A: Liveness: am I stuck and need a restart. Readiness: should I receive traffic right now
options.B: Liveness: CPU saturation. Readiness: memory saturation
options.C: Liveness: can the Service select me. Readiness: can the node schedule me
options.D: Liveness: PVC attached. Readiness: ConfigMap mounted

quiz.explanation: Liveness answers 'restart me.' Readiness answers 'include me in Endpoints.' Mixing them is the classic probe misuse.

quiz.question: You see CrashLoopBackOff on a new Deployment. What does that state actually mean?

options.A: The container started, exited non-zero (or failed liveness), and kubelet is applying exponential backoff before the next restart
options.B: The node is out of CPU and the pod cannot be scheduled
options.C: etcd rejected the pod spec as too large
options.D: The Service has no matching selectors

quiz.explanation: CrashLoopBackOff is a restart policy outcome, not a scheduling failure. kubelet restarts, then waits longer each time (up to a cap) so a broken image does not hammer the node.

quiz.question: During a default rolling update, why can you briefly run more pods than spec.replicas?

options.A: maxSurge allows extra new pods while old pods are still terminating
options.B: HPA always adds 1 replica during any rollout
options.C: etcd duplicates the ReplicaSet until compaction
options.D: kube-proxy clones Endpoints for session affinity

quiz.explanation: RollingUpdate uses maxSurge (extra new) and maxUnavailable (how many can be down). Default surge is why replica count temporarily exceeds the desired count.

quiz.question: A PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable: 2 on a 3-replica app is mainly protecting you from what?

options.A: Voluntary disruptions such as node drains and rolling evictions going below 2 ready pods
options.B: OOMKills and kernel panics on the node
options.C: etcd quorum loss
options.D: Image pull failures from :latest

quiz.explanation: PDBs constrain voluntary disruptions (drain, eviction API, some rolling operations). They do not stop crashes, OOM, or hardware failure.

quiz.question: HPA and VPA solve different bottlenecks. Which pairing is right?

options.A: HPA adds/removes replica count; VPA changes CPU/memory requests (and optionally limits) on the pod
options.B: HPA resizes PVCs; VPA resizes Services
options.C: HPA tunes etcd compaction; VPA tunes kubelet GC
options.D: HPA and VPA are two names for the same controller

quiz.explanation: Horizontal scaling changes how many pods. Vertical scaling changes how big a pod is. Running both aggressively on the same metric fights itself.

quiz.question: The scheduler places pods using which resource field?

options.A: requests — that is the reservation the node must still have free
options.B: limits — that is the only number the scheduler reads
options.C: HPA targetUtilization
options.D: the container image size on disk

quiz.explanation: Scheduling is based on requests (the guaranteed slice). Limits cap runtime usage (CPU throttle or memory OOM) and do not reserve capacity by themselves.

quiz.question: Why is deploying image: myapp:latest a production foot-gun?

options.A: The tag is mutable, so nodes can run different binaries under the same name and rollbacks become guesswork
options.B: Kubernetes refuses to pull tags that are not semver
options.C: :latest disables liveness probes
options.D: etcd cannot store tags named latest

quiz.explanation: latest (any floating tag) is not an immutable content address. imagePullPolicy IfNotPresent can keep a stale local image, or a later pull can silently change what runs.

quiz.question: You kubectl delete a pod. What should the process do in the terminationGracePeriodSeconds window?

options.A: Catch SIGTERM (or preStop), stop taking new work, drain in-flight requests, then exit 0 before the grace period ends
options.B: Ignore signals; kubelet will always wait forever
options.C: Call the HPA API to scale to zero
options.D: Unmount its PVC so other pods can bind it immediately

quiz.explanation: Delete sends SIGTERM after optional preStop. If the process is still running when grace expires, kubelet SIGKILLs it and clients see cut connections.

quiz.question: Every object you kubectl apply is persisted where, and why does that become a cluster bottleneck?

options.A: etcd — it is the consistent store; watch fan-out, large objects, and write bursts all hit it
options.B: Each node's local disk only; the API server is stateless forever
options.C: The container runtime graph driver
options.D: CoreDNS zone files

quiz.explanation: API server is the front door; etcd is the source of truth. Oversized Secrets, high churn, and too many watches make etcd the ceiling for the control plane.

quiz.question: A pod that needs disk should reference a PVC, not a raw disk path. Why?

options.A: PVC is the claim; a PV (often via StorageClass) is the actual volume. Binding decouples app spec from storage backend
options.B: PVCs bypass etcd so disk I/O is faster
options.C: A PVC is just an alias for emptyDir
options.D: Only PVCs can be used with :latest images

quiz.explanation: Pod -> PVC -> PV (provisioned by a StorageClass) is the portable model. The pod should not hard-code cloud volume IDs.

quiz.question: CPU limit is set to 100m, request to 100m. The process tries to use a full core. What do you observe?

options.A: CFS throttling — the container is not OOMKilled for CPU; it just runs slower in bursts
options.B: Immediate CrashLoopBackOff
options.C: The scheduler moves the pod to a bigger node mid-request
options.D: etcd rejects further status updates

quiz.explanation: CPU limits throttle. Memory limits OOMKill. Mixing those failure modes is a common incident-review mistake.

quiz.question: Readiness probe is failing, liveness is passing. User impact?

options.A: Pod stays running but is removed from Service Endpoints, so it gets no new Service traffic
options.B: kubelet SIGKILLs the container every 10s
options.C: The node is cordoned automatically
options.D: PDB is violated and the cluster panics

quiz.explanation: Failed readiness is 'don't send me traffic.' Failed liveness is 'restart me.' That distinction is the whole point of two probes.

quiz.question: A rolling update is stuck: new pods are not Ready, old pods are still serving. Which knob is doing its job?

options.A: The Deployment will not proceed past maxUnavailable / surge until new pods pass readiness — by design
options.B: PDB always blocks Deployment rollouts regardless of replica count
options.C: VPA freezes ReplicaSets during any probe failure
options.D: :latest tags cannot roll forward, only backward

quiz.explanation: Readiness is the gate for rolling updates. If new pods never become Ready, the rollout stalls instead of replacing all healthy pods with broken ones — unless you misconfigured maxUnavailable to allow that.

flashcards.front: Liveness vs readiness, one sentence each
flashcards.back: Liveness: restart this container, it is wedged. Readiness: keep it running but take it out of Endpoints until it can serve. Never point liveness at a shared dependency.

The container keeps dying after start (bad config, missing secret, failed liveness, OOM). kubelet restarts with exponential backoff. Inspect previous logs, exit code, and events — it is not a pending/schedule problem.
maxSurge = extra new pods allowed above desired. maxUnavailable = how many can be down. Together they bound capacity during a Deployment rollout.
Voluntary disruptions (drain, eviction API) that would take ready pods below minAvailable / exceed maxUnavailable. Not node crashes, OOM, or failed liveness.
HPA changes replica count from metrics (CPU, custom). VPA changes resource requests/limits on the pod. They conflict if both chase the same saturation signal.
requests = scheduler reservation and (for CPU) baseline share. limits = runtime cap (CPU throttle, memory OOMKill). A pod with no request can be packed tightly and then starved.

flashcards.front: Why :latest (or any mutable tag) is unsafe
flashcards.back: The name does not pin a digest. Nodes may run different bits, rollbacks are lies, and IfNotPresent may never pick up the 'new latest.' Pin digest or immutable tags.

flashcards.front: Graceful shutdown sequence on pod delete
flashcards.back: preStop hook (if any) → SIGTERM → app drains connections → exit. If still running at terminationGracePeriodSeconds, SIGKILL. Also fail readiness immediately so the Service stops sending work.

quiz.question: An HTTP server needs 30s to warm caches. Liveness and readiness both hit /healthz with failureThreshold: 1 and no initialDelay. Symptom?

options.A: kubelet restarts the container during warmup (liveness) and the pod never joins Endpoints long enough to stay stable
options.B: Only HPA scales to zero
options.C: PVC bind is delayed until the first 200
options.D: etcd compaction deletes the pod spec

quiz.explanation: Startup/warmup belongs to startupProbe or a long initialDelaySeconds on liveness. Using a tight liveness probe during boot is a CrashLoop factory.

quiz.question: You need zero dropped requests during rollout. Besides a correct readiness probe, what else must be true?

options.A: preStop/sleep or SIGTERM drain longer than kube-proxy/Endpoint slice propagation, plus terminationGracePeriodSeconds that covers the drain
options.B: Set maxUnavailable: 100% so old pods vanish instantly
options.C: Use :latest so kubelet always pulls a fresh binary
options.D: Disable PDB so drains are unrestricted

quiz.explanation: Ready=false must happen before the process stops accepting, and the process must keep serving in-flight work until proxies forget the IP. Race those and you 502 during a 'successful' rollout.

quiz.question: A 3-replica Deployment, PDB minAvailable: 3, cluster autoscaler wants to drain a node. What happens?

options.A: Eviction is blocked until extra ready pods exist (or the PDB is loosened); the node drain stalls
options.B: Kubernetes ignores PDB for autoscaler drains
options.C: etcd force-deletes the PDB
options.D: VPA shrinks the pods so three fit on one node automatically

quiz.explanation: minAvailable equal to replica count means zero voluntary disruption. Autoscaler and cluster upgrades get stuck. Leave disruption budget on purpose.

quiz.question: HPA on CPU and VPA in auto mode on the same Deployment. What goes wrong?

options.A: VPA raises requests (CPU looks lower), HPA then scales replicas down (or the reverse) — the two controllers chase each other
options.B: Kubernetes forbids installing both CRDs in one cluster
options.C: etcd stores only HPA or only VPA, never both
options.D: PDB converts all HPAs into VPAs

quiz.explanation: They share the same saturation signal. Typical pattern: HPA for replica count, VPA in recommendation mode only, or VPA for memory with HPA on a custom queue metric.

quiz.question: Burstable pod: request 100Mi, limit 1Gi. Node memory pressure hits. Who dies first among BestEffort / Burstable / Guaranteed?

options.A: BestEffort first, then Burstable that exceeded requests, Guaranteed last — QoS is eviction order, not a fairness scheduler for CPU
options.B: Guaranteed always dies first because it reserved the most
options.C: Only pods without PVCs are evicted
options.D: Eviction order is random by UID

quiz.explanation: QoS (Guaranteed = request==limit for all containers) drives kubelet eviction. Limits without matching requests put you in Burstable, which is cheaper until the node is full.

quiz.question: imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent plus myapp:latest. You push a new latest. A new pod lands on a node that already pulled it last week. Result?

options.A: kubelet reuses the old local image — the new bits never run on that node
options.B: kubelet always re-pulls latest regardless of policy
options.C: The pod CrashLoopBackOffs with ImagePullBackOff
options.D: etcd invalidates the node cache

quiz.explanation: IfNotPresent + mutable tag = sticky old image. AlwaysPull or, better, pin by digest.

quiz.question: A gRPC server ignores SIGTERM. terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30. Clients during Deploy?

options.A: After 30s kubelet SIGKILLs; in-flight RPCs reset. Combined with slow Endpoint removal, you also get connection refused / 502
options.B: kube-proxy holds the connections open indefinitely
options.C: PDB extends the grace period automatically
options.D: HPA intercepts SIGKILL

quiz.explanation: If the app does not drain, grace period is just a delay before a hard kill. Handle SIGTERM and fail readiness first.

quiz.question: Controllers go slow, API list/watch latency climbs, events about etcd timeouts. Highest-leverage first look?

options.A: Object size and write QPS — giant CRDs/Secrets, too many objects, watch storms — etcd disk fsync and DB size
options.B: Whether pods use :latest
options.C: PVC reclaim policy
options.D: HPA sync period only

quiz.explanation: etcd is sensitive to fsync latency, DB size, and expensive watches. Treating it as an app database (huge blobs, high churn) is how control planes die.

quiz.question: Pod mounts a PVC that is already Bound to a PV on another AZ, and the node is in a different AZ. Typical outcome?

options.A: Pod stays Pending (or volume attach fails) — topology and accessMode (RWO) constrain where that claim can run
options.B: kubelet copies the PV across AZs automatically
options.C: etcd replicates block devices
options.D: HPA creates a second PV

quiz.explanation: RWO + zonal disks pin the pod. WaitForFirstConsumer StorageClasses delay binding until a node is chosen for a reason.

quiz.question: maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1, 2 replicas, new image fails readiness. Cluster capacity?

options.A: One extra failing pod may exist; both old Ready pods stay — capacity holds, rollout waits
options.B: Both old pods are killed immediately because surge is 1
options.C: PDB is the only thing that can keep old pods
options.D: VPA deletes the new ReplicaSet

quiz.explanation: maxUnavailable: 0 is the 'never drop capacity' setting. It depends on surge room and readiness of the new pods.

quiz.question: Liveness probe hits / on a server that deadlocks its only thread while still having a listening socket. TCP probe vs HTTP handler probe?

options.A: tcpSocket can still succeed on a deadlocked process; an HTTP (or exec) check of a real handler is required to detect the wedge
options.B: tcpSocket always fails if the app is deadlocked
options.C: Only exec probes can open ports
options.D: Readiness cannot use HTTP

quiz.explanation: A listening socket is not a healthy app. Cheap TCP liveness gives false life. That is probe misuse of a different flavor than 'probe the database.'

quiz.question: OOMKilled, then CrashLoopBackOff. Memory limit is 128Mi, request 128Mi. Fix shape?

options.A: Raise limit (and request if you want Guaranteed) after measuring RSS — the restart loop is the symptom of the cgroup kill, not a probe bug
options.B: Switch the probe from HTTP to TCP so memory is not checked
options.C: Set :latest so a smaller image is pulled
options.D: Add a PDB of minAvailable: 0 to stop OOMs

quiz.explanation: Exit 137 / Reason: OOMKilled is the limit. Probes and PDBs do not add RAM.

quiz.question: You need HPA to scale on queue depth, not CPU. Why is CPU often the wrong signal for that worker?

options.A: A blocked worker can be at 0% CPU with a huge backlog; CPU HPA will scale in and make the queue worse
options.B: HPA cannot use custom metrics in any cluster
options.C: Queue depth is stored only in etcd
options.D: VPA is required before any custom metric

quiz.explanation: Scale on the actual backlog/latency SLO. CPU is a proxy that lies for I/O-bound and lock-bound work.

quiz.question: PV reclaimPolicy Retain vs Delete after PVC is gone. Operational difference?

options.A: Retain leaves the PV and data (Released, manual recover); Delete asks the provisioner to destroy the backing disk
options.B: Retain wipes data; Delete keeps it
options.C: They only affect etcd key TTL
options.D: Reclaim policy changes accessMode from RWO to RWX

quiz.explanation: Delete is convenient and dangerous for stateful data. Retain is how you keep the disk after a namespace/PVC accident.

flashcards.back: 1) Probe a downstream DB/queue. 2) Tight liveness during slow boot (no startupProbe). 3) TCP probe on a deadlocked but listening process. Result: restart storms or silent unhealth.

flashcards.front: Rolling update + readiness + graceful shutdown as one system
flashcards.back: New pod must become Ready before old is dropped (surge/unavailable). Old pod should fail readiness, drain, then exit inside grace. Endpoint propagation lag needs a preStop delay or similar.
minAvailable == replicas blocks drains and some voluntary evictions entirely. You want a budget (e.g. 1 down) so upgrades and autoscaler can move pods.
Both react to CPU/memory saturation. VPA resizing changes utilization, which changes HPA replica math. Prefer one autoscaler on that signal, or split: HPA on traffic, VPA recs for rightsizing.

Every object and watch lands there. Large Secrets/CRDs, thousands of objects per ns, noisy status updates, slow disks. Symptoms: API latency, leader elections, controller lag — not 'the node is slow.'
WaitForFirstConsumer binds after a node is chosen so zonal PVs match. Immediate binding can strand a PVC in the wrong AZ; RWO volumes cannot attach to two nodes.
myapp:v3 or sha256:… is a pin. :latest plus IfNotPresent freezes yesterday's bits; Always plus :latest makes each node a lottery. Controllers and rollbacks need immutability.
Guaranteed: every container request==limit. Burstable: some request. BestEffort: none. Under node memory pressure, BestEffort is evicted first. Limits without requests do not make you Guaranteed.

quiz.question: A mesh sidecar is injected. App readiness is true, sidecar is still warming. Traffic hits the pod and 503s. Root cause class?

options.A: Pod Ready is a conjunction you must encode (aggregate probe / sidecar-aware) — default app-only readiness lies about the data path
options.B: PDB cannot count sidecars so Kubernetes marks Ready anyway
options.C: etcd does not store sidecar status
options.D: HPA always routes to the newest pod

quiz.explanation: Ready means 'the whole pod can serve.' If the proxy is not listening, the app container's 200 is the wrong signal. This is readiness misuse at the pod level.

quiz.question: You set a liveness exec probe that deadlocks on the same global lock as the request path. Failure mode?

options.A: When the app wedges, the probe wedges too; kubelet may restart late or the probe timeout becomes your only detection — and a slow probe can starve other probes
options.B: exec probes run in a separate kernel and cannot deadlock
options.C: kubelet promotes exec to a TCP probe automatically
options.D: VPA kills exec probes

quiz.explanation: Probes must use an independent, cheap path. Sharing locks with the request thread recreates the hang you wanted to detect, or makes kubelet probe workers pile up.

quiz.question: RollingUpdate maxUnavailable: 1 on a StatefulSet of 5 databases, each with a PVC. Why is this not the same as a Deployment surge?

options.A: StatefulSet updates ordinal-by-ordinal, keeps stable network IDs and PVCs; there is no extra surge replica with a new volume — you are trading capacity of that member
options.B: StatefulSet always creates maxSurge extra PVCs
options.C: PDB is ignored for StatefulSets
options.D: :latest is required for ordered pods

quiz.explanation: You cannot 'surge' a unique identity + disk the way you surge stateless pods. Partitioned rolling updates and PDBs are how you keep quorum.

quiz.question: Cluster upgrade drains nodes. App has HPA min=2, PDB minAvailable=50%, and a slow SIGTERM handler (90s) with grace 30s. Incident pattern?

options.A: Drains SIGKILL in-flight work (grace too short) while PDB/HPA still try to keep replica floors — you get both dropped requests and stuck drains
options.B: PDB extends grace to 90s automatically
options.C: HPA disables SIGKILL
options.D: etcd pauses drains until all handlers finish

quiz.explanation: Grace period must exceed drain time. PDB minAvailable must allow a node to empty. Those knobs plus HPA min replicas have to be designed together for upgrades.

quiz.question: VPA recommender suggests 8Gi, HPA target is 70% CPU, Guaranteed QoS. You apply VPA in-place resize where supported vs restart. Risk to availability?

options.A: Resize that needs a restart is an eviction; without surge/PDB room you dip below SLO. In-place CPU/memory still changes utilization and can flap HPA
options.B: VPA never restarts pods in any mode
options.C: Guaranteed QoS blocks all resizes
options.D: etcd stores only the original request forever

quiz.explanation: Vertical change is still a disruption if it recreates the pod. Treat it like a rollout: budget, surge, and don't dual-control the same metric.

quiz.question: A noisy neighbor on a node: your Guaranteed pod has CPU request=limit=1 core but still sees tail latency. Why limits don't isolate you fully?

options.A: CPU limit is CFS quota, not a hard core; last-level cache, noisy disk, and CPU steal still leak. Memory is a cgroup hard cap (OOM), CPU is time slices
options.B: Guaranteed pods pin a physical core by definition
options.C: requests pin the NUMA node and nothing else can run there
options.D: etcd enforces per-pod cache isolation

quiz.explanation: requests/limits are not a hypervisor. For true isolation you need topology/CPU manager policies, separate node pools, or better tenancy — not just matching request to limit.

quiz.question: Admission defaulted imagePullPolicy Always for :latest, but your air-gapped nodes use a rewrite mutating webhook to a digest. A human later kubectl set image …:latest. What breaks first?

options.A: Pulls against a tag that is not in the internal registry, or different nodes resolve different digests if the webhook is skipped on some paths
options.B: Kubernetes converts latest to a digest in etcd forever, so nothing breaks
options.C: PDB blocks all image changes
options.D: HPA refuses to scale pods with latest

quiz.explanation: Policy has to sit on every mutation path (CI, helm, kubectl, operators). :latest is unsafe unless the digest is what is actually recorded on the PodSpec.

quiz.question: preStop sleeps 5s, app drain takes 20s, EndpointSlice propagation p50 is 2s, grace 15s. Still 502s. The math?

options.A: Grace (15) < preStop (5) + drain (20) so SIGKILL cuts the drain; also Ready may still be true during the sleep if you did not fail the probe first
options.B: preStop always runs after SIGKILL
options.C: EndpointSlice propagation cannot cause 502s
options.D: 15s grace is a Kubernetes minimum that cannot SIGKILL

quiz.explanation: terminationGracePeriodSeconds is a hard wall that includes preStop. Fail readiness immediately, size grace to sleep + drain + slack, and don't sleep without dropping Endpoints.

quiz.question: API server / etcd: thousands of Endpoints with notReadyAddresses flapping because readiness is tied to a flappy dependency. Control-plane effect?

options.A: Watch traffic and etcd writes explode (Endpoints/EndpointSlice churn) — you DDoS the control plane with probe misuse
options.B: etcd ignores Endpoint updates
options.C: Only kube-proxy on that node is affected; API QPS is unchanged
options.D: VPA compresses Endpoint objects

quiz.explanation: Readiness flaps are not just user 502s. They write objects. At scale this is how a bad probe becomes an etcd incident.

quiz.question: Two pods, ReadWriteOnce PVC, StatefulSet replica 2, same StorageClass. Why the second pod is Pending?

options.A: Each ordinal needs its own PVC (volumeClaimTemplates). Sharing one RWO claim is invalid; the volume attaches to at most one node
options.B: StatefulSet requires RWX for replica 0 only
options.C: Pending means CrashLoopBackOff
options.D: HPA must create PVCs and it is not installed

quiz.explanation: RWO = one attacher. Scale-out stateful apps get one PVC per pod via templates, or an RWX filesystem with a clear consistency story.

quiz.question: You mark a Deployment progressDeadlineSeconds too low while image pulls are slow. Interaction with rolling update?

options.A: The rollout is marked failed (Progressing=false) even though pods might still become Ready — automation may abort or rollback while surge pods exist
options.B: progressDeadline pauses etcd
options.C: It only affects CronJobs
options.D: It overrides PDB

quiz.explanation: Rollout success is a time-bounded condition. Tight deadlines plus slow pulls/readiness look like a failed rollout even when the strategy math is fine.

quiz.question: Memory-backed emptyDir plus a container memory limit. Process writes a huge file to the volume. Who kills it?

options.A: The emptyDir counts against the pod's memory cgroup — you can OOMKill without a 'real' leak in the heap
options.B: emptyDir is always disk and cannot OOM
options.C: Only PVCs count toward limits
options.D: kubelet moves the file to the PV automatically

quiz.explanation: medium: Memory is tmpfs in the memory cgroup. Limits apply. This shows up as mysterious OOMs next to 'but RSS looked fine in the app metric.'

quiz.question: You need disruption-safe cluster autoscaler + PDB + HPA. Which invariant is the one that actually allows a node to go away?

options.A: After a pod is evicted, HPA/scheduler can place a replacement elsewhere AND the PDB still holds on remaining Ready pods — if utilization is so tight no extra pod can schedule, drains deadlock
options.B: PDB guarantees a new node is created first in all cases
options.C: HPA minReplicas always includes surge nodes
options.D: etcd reserves one empty node per PDB

quiz.explanation: PDBs do not create capacity. If the cluster is packed to 100% requests, voluntary disruption cannot proceed. Headroom is part of the PDB design.

quiz.question: Secret stored as a whole kubeconfig in etcd, updated every minute by an operator, mounted in 200 pods. Primary harm?

options.A: Huge, hot objects in etcd plus mount/watch storms on every kubelet — control plane and node I/O, not just 'a secret rotated'
options.B: PVCs cannot mount Secrets
options.C: HPA will scale to 200 automatically
options.D: :latest will be rewritten into the Secret

quiz.explanation: etcd is a small consistent store. Treating it as a blob store for frequently mutated large objects is the textbook bottleneck. Externalize blobs; keep etcd keys small and rare.

flashcards.front: Readiness must describe the data path
flashcards.back: Include sidecars, listen ports, and warmup. App /healthz 200 while the proxy is down still blackholes Service traffic. Flappy readiness also churns EndpointSlices in etcd.

flashcards.front: startupProbe vs lying with delayed liveness
flashcards.back: startupProbe disables liveness/readiness until boot succeeds (with its own failure budget). A long initialDelay on liveness is a cruder version and still leaves a dead-during-delay window.
Identities and disks do not surge. PDB must protect quorum (e.g. majority of members Ready). RWO volumes pin AZ/node; drains need replacement capacity in the same topology.
Clock starts at deletion. preStop sleep + app drain must fit. Fail readiness first so Endpoints drop while you still serve in-flight. Then SIGKILL is a last resort, not the plan.
Probe flaps, status spam, huge CRDs/Secrets, per-pod objects with high churn. You will see API latency and etcd fsync saturation before you see 'the Deployment is slow.'
HPA wants replicas, VPA wants restarts/resizes, PDB wants a Ready floor, cluster autoscaler wants to drain. If requests fill every node, nothing voluntary can move. Design headroom.

flashcards.front: Image identity that CI and cluster agree on
flashcards.back: Record image@sha256 in the PodSpec. Webhooks that rewrite :latest must run on kubectl, operators, and CI alike. Mixed pull policies across nodes produce split-brain binaries.

Retain: Released PV needs manual claimRef clear to reuse. Delete: provisioner destroys data. WaitForFirstConsumer vs Immediate. RWO attach to one node. tmpfs emptyDir counts as memory against the limit.

quiz.question: You need 'get user by id' at huge QPS, ids are arbitrary strings, no range queries. Which shape fits the workload?

options.A: Hash table (average O(1) point lookup) — a tree adds comparison overhead you do not need, a heap is not a dictionary
options.B: Binary heap, because it always stores the minimum id on top
options.C: Linked list, because pointers are faster than arrays
options.D: DFS forest, because ids form a graph

quiz.explanation: Point lookup by exact key is the hash table job. Trees win when you need ordered scans or predecessor. Heaps win when you need extract-min, not search-by-key.

quiz.question: Why do textbook linked-list queues often lose to a ring buffer of the same logical operations on real hardware?

options.A: Each node is a separate allocation; pointer chasing misses cache and TLB, while a contiguous buffer hits cache lines and prefetches
options.B: Linked lists have worse big-O for enqueue than arrays in the RAM model
options.C: CPUs cannot follow pointers at all
options.D: The kernel refuses to allocate list nodes

quiz.explanation: Big-O counts pointer operations, not cache misses. A list 'O(1) insert' can be far slower than compact array work that the CPU actually likes.

quiz.question: A Bloom filter says 'this user id is not in the set.' What can you conclude?

options.A: It is definitely not in the set — Bloom filters have false positives, not false negatives (for a static membership filter)
options.B: It might still be in the set; negatives are probabilistic
options.C: You must re-hash with a tree to confirm negatives
options.D: The filter is corrupted whenever it says no

quiz.explanation: Standard Bloom: 'no' is certain, 'yes' means 'maybe — check the source of truth.' That is the whole product contract.

quiz.question: You add a cache node and want existing keys to mostly stay put. Why not hash(key) % N?

options.A: Changing N remaps almost every key; consistent hashing (or Rendezvous) moves only a ~1/N fraction
options.B: Modulo is cryptographically unsafe, so caches reject it
options.C: % N cannot be computed for strings
options.D: Heaps cannot store the modulus

quiz.explanation: The operational cost is cache stampedes and data movement, not the CPU cost of modulo. Consistent hashing exists to stabilize ownership under membership change.

quiz.question: An LRU cache is hit on every request for a hot key. What must the structure do in O(1) expected time?

options.A: Hash map to the node plus a recency list (or equivalent) so lookup, move-to-front, and eviction of the tail are cheap
options.B: Scan the whole array to find the oldest timestamp
options.C: Rebuild a heap from scratch on every hit
options.D: BFS the keyspace

quiz.explanation: LRU is 'dictionary + recency order.' Map alone has no order; list alone has slow find. Together they match the workload.

quiz.question: You need the shortest number of hops in an unweighted graph (site crawler, maze). BFS or DFS?

options.A: BFS — the first time you reach a node is a minimum-hop path; DFS can dive down a long dead end first
options.B: DFS — recursion always yields shortest paths
options.C: Either, because both visit the same nodes
options.D: A heap of random nodes

quiz.explanation: Unweighted shortest path is the BFS workload. DFS is for reachability, topological-style exploration, and some memory tricks — not hop distance.

quiz.question: You sort invoices by date, then by customer, and you need all of one customer's invoices to stay in date order. What property do you need from the second sort?

options.A: Stability — equal keys (same customer) keep their previous (date) order
options.B: In-place partitioning
options.C: That the sort is a heap sort, which is always stable
options.D: Bloom-filter uniqueness of dates

quiz.explanation: Stable sort is why multi-key sorting by successive passes works. Unstable sorts scramble the earlier key among ties.

quiz.question: You have n chat rooms and union operations 'merge these two rooms' plus 'are these users in the same room?' Which structure?

options.A: Union-find (disjoint-set) with path compression / union by rank
options.B: A max-heap of room ids
options.C: BFS from user 0 on every query
options.D: A Bloom filter of pairs

quiz.explanation: Dynamic connectivity with unions is union-find's workload. A heap does not answer 'same component.' Repeated BFS is the slow version of the same idea.

quiz.question: You need the next job with the highest priority, repeatedly, while jobs arrive. Hash, tree, or heap?

options.A: Heap (priority queue) — extract-max/min is the operation; a hash has no order, an ordered tree can do it but with more overhead if you only need the extreme
options.B: Hash table keyed by priority, because priorities are unique
options.C: Singly linked list scanned from the head only
options.D: Bloom filter of finished jobs

quiz.explanation: Match the structure to the query: 'give me the extreme, then the next.' That is a heap. Need delete-arbitrary and successor too? Then a tree (or heap+map).

quiz.question: A Bloom filter says 'yes, this email was seen.' You skip sending. Risk?

options.A: False positive — you may skip a never-seen email; if skips are costly, store a real set or a cache in front of source of truth
options.B: False negative — Bloom filters invent missing emails
options.C: Union-find will correct it on the next hop
options.D: LRU will convert the maybe into a no

quiz.explanation: Product choice: Bloom is for cheap negative checks (don't hit disk if definitely absent). Using the 'yes' as ground truth is the false-positive bug.

quiz.question: DFS vs BFS for 'does a path exist in a huge, deep, narrow maze if you are memory-constrained'?

options.A: DFS uses stack proportional to depth, which can be smaller than BFS's frontier in a wide graph — but it can also go infinitely deep without extra guards
options.B: BFS always uses less memory than DFS
options.C: They use identical memory on every graph
options.D: Only union-find can test connectivity

quiz.explanation: Pick BFS/DFS by what you need (shortest vs any path) and by the shape of the frontier vs the depth. Memory is a workload constraint, not a trivia identity.

quiz.question: You iterate a large array of structs vs a linked list of the same structs, summing one field. Why is the array usually much faster?

options.A: Sequential access prefetches; the list jumps to heap allocations that evict useful cache lines
options.B: Arrays have better big-O for a linear scan than lists
options.C: Linked lists cannot store structs
options.D: The compiler forbids summing list nodes

quiz.explanation: Both are linear scans in the RAM model. Hardware makes locality the real complexity.

quiz.question: Consistent hashing places both keys and nodes on a ring. A node dies. What should happen to its keys?

options.A: They move to the next node(s) on the ring (or to replicas), not to a random reshuffle of the whole keyspace
options.B: Every key is rehashed with % (N-1)
options.C: A Bloom filter deletes the node
options.D: LRU evicts all keys cluster-wide

quiz.explanation: Local movement is the point. Virtual nodes exist to even out the slice sizes when physical nodes are few.

quiz.question: You sort a list of (name, score) by score descending with an unstable sort, then by name. What breaks?

options.A: People with the same name no longer keep score order from the first pass — the second key scramble depends on stability of the name sort
options.B: Unstable sorts cannot compare integers
options.C: Heaps cannot sort pairs
options.D: BFS will restore the score order

quiz.explanation: If you compose sorts, each pass except the last must be stable (or you sort by a composite key in one pass). Stability is a product requirement, not a curiosity.

flashcards.front: Pick hash vs tree vs heap from the query
flashcards.back: Exact key lookup / membership → hash. Ordered range, predecessor, sorted iteration → tree. Repeated extract-min/max → heap. Do not store a dictionary in a heap.

flashcards.front: Why linked lists lose on real machines
flashcards.back: Pointer chasing: poor spatial locality, extra allocations, no prefetch. An array/ring buffer does the same O(1) enqueue with contiguous loads. Measure cache misses, not just big-O.
'No' = definitely absent. 'Yes' = maybe present (false positives). Size and hash count trade memory for that error rate. Never treat yes as proof.
hash % N reshuffles nearly all keys when N changes. Consistent hashing moves ~keys/N. Use it for caches, shards, and DHT-style ownership.
Hash map: key → node. Doubly linked list (or clock/2Q variant): recency. Hit = splice to front. Evict = drop tail. One without the other misses the workload.

flashcards.front: BFS vs DFS, pick from the question
flashcards.back: Fewest hops / unweighted shortest / level order → BFS. Explore one branch, cycle detect in directed graphs, topo-style recursion, lower memory on skinny graphs → DFS.

flashcards.front: When stability of a sort matters
flashcards.back: Ties must keep input order: multi-pass sorts (sort by last key first), UI that should not jump rows, and merging already-ordered groups. Unstable is fine if you sort a total unique key.
Disjoint sets with merge and same-component queries (networks, Kruskal, clustering). Path compression + union by rank makes the operations effectively tiny. Not a replacement for shortest path.

quiz.question: Workload: 10M keys, need 'all keys between A and B' and occasional insert. Engineer proposes a hash map. What fails?

options.A: Hashes do not keep order — range scan becomes a full table scan; an ordered tree (or B-tree / LSM with keys in order) matches the scan
options.B: Hash maps cannot insert after construction
options.C: Trees cannot store 10M keys
options.D: A heap can range-scan in sorted order without extra cost

quiz.explanation: Match access pattern: ranges want ordered layout. Hash is the wrong invariant, even if point get would be faster.

quiz.question: You implement LRU with a hash map plus singly linked list. Evict-the-tail is easy; a hit in the middle is not O(1). Missing piece?

options.A: You need a back pointer (doubly linked) or an explicit prev in the map so you can unlink in O(1)
options.B: Singly linked lists are always O(1) to move a middle node
options.C: A Bloom filter of the tail replaces the list
options.D: BFS from the head on each hit is the standard LRU

quiz.explanation: O(1) LRU is about unlinking. Singly linked + no prev forces a scan. This is a structure-vs-workload miss, not a 'linked lists are slow' slogan.

quiz.question: Bloom filter at 1% false positive, you then always fetch the DB on 'yes.' What did you actually save?

options.A: Negative lookups skip the DB; positives (true and false) still pay the DB round trip — win is skewed to mostly-miss workloads
options.B: You saved the DB on all yes answers
options.C: False positives delete DB rows
options.D: The filter replaces the DB for yes and no

quiz.explanation: Bloom is a negative cache in front of a source of truth. If the workload is almost all hits, it barely helps and still costs CPU/memory.

quiz.question: Consistent hashing without virtual nodes, 3 physical caches of unequal capacity. Typical pain?

options.A: Arc sizes are lumpy — one node owns a huge key range; virtual nodes (many labels per physical) smooth load
options.B: All keys hash to node 0 by definition
options.C: Union-find is required to split the ring
options.D: LRU cannot run on a ring

quiz.explanation: The ring is fair only in expectation with enough points. Virtual nodes (or bounded loads / jump hashing) are how you make it operationally even.

quiz.question: Graph of a social network: find people within 2 hops. Why BFS beats DFS here?

options.A: You care about distance layers; BFS emits level 1 then 2 and can stop. DFS can wander to hop 40 before it has finished hop 2
options.B: DFS cannot mark visited nodes
options.C: BFS cannot handle cycles
options.D: Heaps compute hop count faster than queues

quiz.explanation: The query is a ball around a node. BFS is layered. DFS would need extra distance bookkeeping and still does extra work.

quiz.question: You must sort 1e8 records that are already almost sorted by timestamp, and equal timestamps must not reorder events. Which concern dominates?

options.A: Stability (and preferably an algorithm that is fast on nearly-ordered input) — a random-swap unstable sort both scrambles ties and fights the existing order
options.B: Only whether the textbook name is merge sort
options.C: Converting to a linked list first for locality
options.D: Inserting into a Bloom filter then iterating it

quiz.explanation: The requirement is 'do not reorder equal keys, and don't shuffle a nearly-sorted stream.' That is stability plus adaptivity — not reciting an algorithm's classroom bound.

quiz.question: Online connectivity: unions arrive, and you also need the size of each component. Union-find tweak?

options.A: Store subtree/component size on the root; union by size and add sizes on merge — queries read the root's size after find
options.B: Run BFS from every node after each union
options.C: Put components in a max-heap keyed by an arbitrary id
options.D: Hash each pair of nodes

quiz.explanation: Augment the root. That is the usual way union-find carries extra aggregates (size, min, parity).

quiz.question: A priority queue of tasks also needs 'cancel task by id.' Plain binary heap problem?

options.A: Find-by-id is not a heap operation — keep a hash from id → heap index (or a tree of tasks) so decrease-key/delete is possible
options.B: Heaps already index by arbitrary id
options.C: Cancel is a BFS of the heap array
options.D: Use a Bloom filter as the heap

quiz.explanation: Heap = partial order for the extreme. Dictionary = identity. Real schedulers compose them (or use an ordered tree).

quiz.question: You store a graph as adjacency lists of linked nodes, then BFS a high-degree vertex. Hardware issue?

options.A: The neighbor list itself pointer-chases; a compact CSR/adjacency array scans neighbors in cache-line bursts and BFS gets faster without changing the algorithm
options.B: BFS is impossible without linked lists
options.C: DFS requires arrays; BFS requires lists
options.D: Union-find will pack the lists

quiz.explanation: Same graph algorithm, different layout. Locality of the frontier and of adjacency is why some BFS implementations crush others.

quiz.question: Cache with consistent hashing. Client hashes to node A; A misses and fills from DB. Node A is added/removed and the key now lives on B, which is empty. User-visible issue?

options.A: Those keys thundering-herd the DB until B fills — consistent hashing reduces movement but does not zero it; replicas/shadow fills exist for that
options.B: Consistent hashing forbids misses after a membership change
options.C: LRU on B automatically contains A's memory
options.D: Bloom filters migrate the bytes

quiz.explanation: Ownership move ≠ data move. Plan for a miss storm on the receiving node.

quiz.question: You need a set-membership check in a scraper: 'have I already queued this URL?' Memory is tight, duplicates are annoying but not fatal. Structure?

options.A: Bloom filter (accept some extra fetches) — a hash set of all URLs may not fit; a tree of URLs is even heavier
options.B: A heap of URLs ordered by length
options.C: DFS stack as the only store
options.D: Union-find on characters of the URL

quiz.explanation: False positives here mean 'skip a URL that was new' (lost work) or you invert the sense: use Bloom to skip known-seen if you only insert after success. Tune which error you accept.

quiz.question: A UI table sorts by selected column. Rows with equal values jump around every click. Users complain. Fix?

options.A: Use a stable sort, or add a hidden unique tie-breaker (original index) so the order is deterministic
options.B: Switch from array to linked list of rows
options.C: BFS the table model
options.D: Put rows in a Bloom filter

quiz.explanation: Stability (or an explicit unique key) is UX. Unstable in-place sorts reshuffle ties because equal keys may swap.

quiz.question: Kruskal-style clustering: merge closest pairs until k clusters. Why union-find instead of rerunning DFS?

options.A: Each merge and 'same cluster?' is cheap with disjoint sets; DFS from scratch every edge is repeating connectivity work
options.B: DFS cannot detect connected components
options.C: Heaps find components faster than union-find
options.D: Bloom filters cluster by hash collisions on purpose

quiz.explanation: The algorithm's inner loop is dynamic connectivity. Union-find is that loop. Pair it with a heap/sort of edges if you also need 'closest.'

quiz.question: Hash table vs balanced tree for a language runtime dictionary. Hash is faster on average. When do you still pick the tree?

options.A: You need worst-case bounds, ordered iteration, or keys that are expensive/adversarial to hash — trees give comparable keys an order hash does not
options.B: Trees always beat hashes on point lookup
options.C: Heaps iterate in hash order
options.D: Linked lists iterate faster than both

quiz.explanation: Average vs worst case, and extra operations (lower_bound). The workload, not the classroom 'hash is O(1),' decides.

flashcards.back: Point: hash. Range/predecessor/in-order: tree (in memory) or B-tree/LSM (on disk). Heap only gives you the current extreme, not a range.
Map to node + doubly linked recency list (or indexed array). Singly linked forces scans. Clock/2Q trade exact LRU for fewer pointer writes — still a layout choice.

flashcards.front: Bloom pays off on negative-heavy traffic
flashcards.back: Each 'no' avoids a slower check. Each 'yes' still goes to source of truth, including false positives. Size the filter from n and target error; rebuild or counting variants if deletes matter.

flashcards.front: Virtual nodes on a hash ring
flashcards.back: Many tokens per physical server so ranges are small and mix well. Unequal capacity → proportional token count. Still plan warmup when a token range moves.
Wide shallow graphs: BFS queue can explode (social hops). Deep graphs: DFS stack can explode. Bidirectional BFS shrinks the frontier for shortest paths between two nodes.

flashcards.front: Stable sort as a product feature
flashcards.back: Preserve earlier sort keys; keep original row order on ties; merge sorted runs without scrambling equals. If you need a total order, add a unique tie-break instead of hoping.
Keep aggregates on the root (size, min id, XOR, bipartite parity). After find, both nodes share a root so the payload is the component's. Rebuild payload on union.
extract-min is fast; find/cancel by id is not unless you add a hash of indices or use a tree. Schedulers, Dijkstra decrease-key, and timers all hit this.

quiz.question: Hot-key workload: 1 key is 40% of QPS. Hash partition across 50 caches. What structure-level fact did you ignore?

options.A: Hashing spreads keys, not load — one key still lives on one shard; you need replication, local LRU on every node, or a different split (by session, by request) for that key
options.B: A balanced tree on the same key automatically shards it
options.C: A heap of caches will split the key each extract-min
options.D: Consistent hashing splits a single key across the ring by definition

quiz.explanation: Partitioning is per key. Hot keys are a workload the hash cannot save you from. Trees and heaps do not change that.

quiz.question: You replace an array-backed deque with a linked list to get 'true O(1) insert in the middle' for a 1e7-element structure you mostly iterate. Net effect on a modern CPU?

options.A: Middle insert may allocate and patch two pointers, but iteration becomes cache-hostile; if iterates dominate, you slowed the real workload
options.B: Linked lists always dominate arrays once n > 10^4
options.C: The allocator colocates list nodes so they prefetch like arrays
options.D: TLB prefers pointer graphs to contiguous pages

quiz.explanation: Optimize for the common operation and for locality. 'O(1) middle insert' is irrelevant if you almost never insert in the middle and you scan constantly.

quiz.question: Counting Bloom / cuckoo / quotient filters exist. You need deletes and a hard bound on false positives for a security denylist. Why a vanilla Bloom is the wrong contract?

options.A: Standard Bloom cannot delete safely and never gives 0% false positives — a 'yes' could allow or deny the wrong principal; use an exact set or a structure with bounded, understood errors
options.B: Vanilla Bloom has false negatives, which are worse for denylists
options.C: Union-find can delete Bloom bits
options.D: LRU turns Bloom into an exact set

quiz.explanation: Security denylist: false negative (missing a bad id) or false positive (blocking a good id) are product bugs. Bloom's maybe-yes is the wrong invariant unless you always fall back to exact check.

quiz.question: Rendezvous hashing vs consistent ring: you want minimal disruption and easy weighted nodes without virtual node explosion. Which idea?

options.A: Highest random weight / Rendezvous: score(key, node), pick max — membership change only moves keys that preferred the lost node; weights fold into the score
options.B: Always use hash % N with sticky sessions
options.C: Put nodes in a heap and extract-min per key
options.D: DFS the node list until a Bloom filter says yes

quiz.explanation: Same goal as consistent hashing (stable ownership), different math. Rings need many vnodes for balance; HRW weights naturally. Both still don't split a hot key.

quiz.question: LRU under scan-heavy traffic (a job reads every key once). What happens to the cache of hot keys?

options.A: The scan fills the recency list and evicts the working set — classic LRU failure; use scan-resistant policy (2Q, ARC, LRU-K) or pin/hot-bit
options.B: LRU is scan-proof because hashes skip one-time keys
options.C: A heap ordered by key length stops scans
options.D: BFS insertion order is immune

quiz.explanation: LRU assumes recency predicts reuse. A sequential scan violates that. The structure still 'works'; the replacement policy is wrong for the workload.

quiz.question: Directed graph, detect if adding an edge would create a cycle, online, many queries. DFS every time is too slow. Better?

options.A: If the graph is a DAG of components you merge, union-find works for undirected; for directed you need incremental topo / reachability (or full topo + DFS on the relevant region) — union-find alone is the wrong connectivity model
options.B: Union-find is identical for directed cycles
options.C: A Bloom filter of edges proves acyclicity
options.D: BFS from a random node never sees directed cycles

quiz.explanation: Union-find is undirected disjoint sets. Directed cycle detection is reachability. Using the wrong connectivity structure is a common 'I know union-find' miss.

quiz.question: You external-sort huge files. Runs are written, then merged. Why does 'stable' still matter on disk?

options.A: Equal keys from earlier files/runs must keep their input order (e.g. original row id, replica timestamp) or the merge invents a new ordering that downstream consumers did not ask for
options.B: Stability only exists in RAM arrays, not files
options.C: Heaps used in k-way merge are stable by nature for all equal keys
options.D: BFS merge of runs preserves order automatically

quiz.explanation: A k-way heap merge is not stable unless you add a tie-break (run index, original offset). Stability is an extra key you encode, not a magic property of 'merge.'

quiz.question: Dijkstra on a huge sparse graph: binary heap vs array vs Fibonacci-style vs just BFS. Workload split?

options.A: If all weights are equal, BFS (or 0-1 deque) — a heap is wasted. If weights vary, you need a PQ; which PQ depends on decrease-key volume and graph size, not the brand name
options.B: Always Fibonacci heap because the bound is famous
options.C: DFS with a Bloom filter replaces Dijkstra
options.D: Union-find extracts the next closest node

quiz.explanation: Equal weights → BFS. Positive varying weights → PQ. The structure follows the weight model. Do not import a heap because the textbook picture had one.

quiz.question: CHAMP / HAMT / B-tree vs open-addressing hash for a persistent (immutable) map in a language runtime. Why the tree-like hash trie?

options.A: Structural sharing on update: you copy a path, not the whole table — a flat hash array maps poorly onto persistent workloads even if lookups are similar
options.B: Trees cannot share structure
options.C: Open addressing is required for immutability
options.D: Heaps persist better because extract-min copies nothing

quiz.explanation: Workload is 'copy-on-write map with many versions.' Layout and sharing beat a slightly faster ephemeral hash.

quiz.question: False-positive rate of a Bloom filter after you insert more items than it was sized for. What actually happens?

options.A: Bits saturate, 'yes' becomes almost always — the filter silently degrades toward useless; there is no crash, which is why ops miss it
options.B: It starts emitting false negatives to compensate
options.C: Union-find rebuilds the bitset
options.D: LRU evicts bits in recency order

quiz.explanation: Capacity is part of the contract. Overfill does not throw; it lies more. Monitor fill and rebuild/rotate filters.

quiz.question: You need an LRU across a fleet. Local LRU per node + consistent hashing. A key's node jumps; the new node has a cold LRU. Besides miss storm, what invariant broke?

options.A: Recency is per process — the global working set is not on the ring. Hashing moves identity, not the linked-list order; replicas or session stickiness are how you keep recency
options.B: Consistent hashing copies the doubly linked list to the successor automatically
options.C: A heap of timestamps is globally shared via hashing
options.D: BFS of the ring rebuilds LRU

quiz.explanation: Two structures, two jobs. The ring assigns owners; LRU is local memory order. Don't expect one to implement the other.

quiz.question: Union-find with path compression, no union-by-rank, adversarial unions always attaching large to small via the wrong root. Practical issue?

options.A: Trees get tall; even with later compression, a bad sequence plus no rank/size can make individual finds scan long chains before they flatten
options.B: Path compression without rank is undefined
options.C: The structure becomes a heap and extract-min breaks
options.D: Bloom filter bits collide with the parent array

quiz.explanation: The pairing of compression + rank/size is what keeps forests flat in the real sequences you get before compression runs. Production UF uses both.

quiz.question: A 'linked list of buffers' vs a small number of large slabs for a network server. Same abstract list of bytes. Why slabs?

options.A: Fewer allocations, sequential DMA/cache, cheaper to coalesce; the pointer-rich list maximizes syscall and miss cost per byte
options.B: The kernel can only send linked lists
options.C: Slabs cannot represent a queue
options.D: BFS requires one malloc per byte

quiz.explanation: This is the linked-list-vs-hardware lesson at systems scale: iovecs/slabs/rings, not node-per-object, unless the object lifetimes truly demand it.

quiz.question: You sort events by (user_id, event_time) for per-user sessionization. One-pass composite compare vs sort-by-time then stable sort-by-user. When is the two-pass actually what you want?

options.A: When event_time order among a user must be the original sort's order and that first sort was already done (or is expensive to redo as a composite) — stability composes existing order; a new unstable composite can still break equal (user, time) ties you cared about
options.B: Two-pass is always slower and never justified
options.C: Heaps can only do one key
options.D: BFS requires two-pass sorts

quiz.explanation: Composite keys are usually cleaner. Two-pass + stable is how you reuse an existing ordering or add a key without rewriting the comparator. Either way you must define tie-breaks on purpose.

flashcards.back: One hot key hashes to one owner. Consistent hashing, trees, and heaps do not split that key. Replicate it, split by a finer workload key, or keep it in a special cache.

flashcards.front: Locality is the real 'complexity' of lists
flashcards.back: Node-per-element structures lose to arrays, rings, CSR graphs, and slab buffers because of cache, TLB, allocator, and prefetch. Use links when identity and splice truly dominate scans.

flashcards.front: Bloom overfill and the security misuse
flashcards.back: Over-inserting → bits fill → almost every query is 'yes.' For denylist/allow decisions, 'maybe' is not an answer unless an exact check follows. Deletes need a different filter.
% N reshuffles everything. Ring + vnodes: local moves, watch load lumps. Rendezvous/HRW: per-key max score, natural weights, no vnode explosion. None of them move payload bytes for you.
The map+list is O(1) recency. The policy still fails on scans and one-hit wonders. ARC/2Q/W-TinyLFU change who gets evicted without changing 'we need a dictionary.'
Union-find = undirected components. Shortest hops = BFS (unweighted) or PQ (weighted). Directed cycles = reachability/topo, not disjoint sets. Pick the invariant, then the structure.

flashcards.front: Stability as an extra sort key
flashcards.back: Heap merge and many in-place sorts are not stable. Encode original index / run id in the comparator. Multi-key sorts are either one composite compare or stable passes from last key to first.

flashcards.front: Compose structures for the real API
flashcards.back: Scheduler: heap + hash (cancel). LRU: hash + list. Kruskal: sort/heap of edges + union-find. Cache cluster: consistent hash + local LRU + Bloom negative cache. One textbook type is rarely the product.
